<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-yogurt" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-yogurt-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of yogurt, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>59</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>FDA Total Diet Study</td><td>6</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>authors 2025</td><td>1</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>Nwoke et al. 2021</td><td>3</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>Rebellato et al. 2023</td><td>1</td><td>17%</td></tr><tr><td>Spungen et al. 2024</td><td>1</td><td>17%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for yogurt, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. Other forms, other bases, targeted sampling and results from mining, industrial, wastewater-affected, experimental, fertiliser or manufacturer settings are kept out of this reference.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>6 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach yogurt

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach yogurt comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Yogurt, as sold from commercial/retail, conventional, packaged had total arsenic higher at 3.6 µg/kg, against 1 µg/kg for Buffalo yogurt (farm-origin, Certeze area) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Marcus OI, Tabaran A, Crisan Reget OL, Dan SD, Panait LC, Lacatus CM, Popescu M, Codea AR, Purdoiu RC, Lacatus R, Petrescu-Mag IV, Nicolescu A, Bora FD · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms">From Farm to Retail: Decoding the Elemental Landscape of Milk and Dairy Products Across Organic and Conventional Production Systems Using ICP-MS</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics 2026, 14, 124</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.

<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into yogurt?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, yogurt from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than yogurt from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Marcus OI, Tabaran A, Crisan Reget OL, Dan SD, Panait LC, Lacatus CM, Popescu M, Codea AR, Purdoiu RC, Lacatus R, Petrescu-Mag IV, Nicolescu A, Bora FD · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms">From Farm to Retail: Decoding the Elemental Landscape of Milk and Dairy Products Across Organic and Conventional Production Systems Using ICP-MS</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics 2026, 14, 124</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Yogurt, as sold from commercial/retail, conventional, packaged had total arsenic higher at 3.6 µg/kg, against 1 µg/kg for Buffalo yogurt (farm-origin, Certeze area) in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Marcus OI, Tabaran A, Crisan Reget OL, Dan SD, Panait LC, Lacatus CM, Popescu M, Codea AR, Purdoiu RC, Lacatus R, Petrescu-Mag IV, Nicolescu A, Bora FD · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms">From Farm to Retail: Decoding the Elemental Landscape of Milk and Dairy Products Across Organic and Conventional Production Systems Using ICP-MS</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics 2026, 14, 124</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/marcus2026-organic-conventional-dairy-icpms">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-yogurt" data-anchor="which-regions-report-the-lowest-levels-in-yogurt" data-question="Which regions report the lowest levels in yogurt?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which regions report the lowest levels in yogurt?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Among GEMS/Food reporting regions, yogurt, as sold had the lowest lead subgroup median in WPRO (2.5 µg/kg) and the highest in WPRO (5.5 µg/kg); reporting regions are markets, not growing areas.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-yogurt-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-yogurt-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in yogurt is inorganic?">
